class: One of the possible answers a network can choose between, like fruit, chips or cookie.
cross-entropy: A loss for networks that output probabilities: minus the log of the probability the model gave to the right answer, so confident mistakes cost the most.
squared error: A simple loss: the gap between the truth and the prediction, multiplied by itself, so bigger misses count much more.
derivative: The slope of a curve at one point: how fast the output changes when the input changes a tiny bit.
saturated: Describes a sigmoid neuron pushed so far to one end that its curve is almost flat, so it barely learns.
hyperparameter: A setting chosen by the person building the network before training starts, like the learning rate or the number of hidden neurons.
gradient descent: The learning rule: find the slope of the loss for every weight, then move each weight a small step in the downhill direction.
loss landscape: A picture of the loss for every possible setting of the weights: hills where the network is wrong, valleys where it does well.
local minimum: A dip in the loss landscape that is lower than everything right next to it but is not the lowest point overall.
momentum: Gradient descent with a memory: each step keeps most of the previous step's velocity, so steady slopes build up speed.
Adam: The most widely used training method: momentum plus an automatic step size for every weight.
mini-batch: A small handful of training examples used to work out one quick, roughly right gradient step.
stochastic gradient descent: Gradient descent that takes each step using a random mini-batch instead of the whole training set.
standardize: To rescale a column of inputs so its average is 0 and its spread is about 1, which puts every input on an equal footing.
standard deviation: A measure of how spread out a set of numbers is around their average.
baseline: The score you would get with no skill at all, such as by guessing. A result only means something compared with it.
universal approximation theorem: A proof that one hidden layer can fit almost any shape if it is wide enough. It says nothing about how to find the weights.
tanh: An activation shaped like sigmoid that outputs between −1 and +1 instead of 0 and 1.
scaling law: A measured rule for how a model's performance improves as its size, data and computing grow.
GPU: A graphics chip with thousands of simple cores that can do huge numbers of small sums at the same time, which is what neural networks need.
residual connection: A shortcut that lets a signal skip past a layer, which keeps gradients alive in very deep networks.
